notes:
User is learning Python through Corey Schafer’s YouTube programming series and has completed 30 videos. They plan to begin DataCamp’s introductory NLP course and want practical project guidance. They have started thinking about a beginner NLP project involving text analysis and sentiment analysis, likely using IMDB Movie Reviews or Amazon product reviews.

Recommended learning path: first build a sentiment classifier using preprocessing, train/test splits, simple features (bag-of-words or TF-IDF), a baseline such as logistic regression, and evaluation with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. Useful libraries/tools include NLTK, spaCy, gensim, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, Jupyter, VS Code, Git, and virtual environments. Suggested environment structure includes `data/`, `models/`, `notebooks/`, `src/`, and `requirements.txt`.

After becoming comfortable with sentiment analysis, user wants to explore NER, topic modeling, POS tagging, dependency parsing, and other NLP techniques. They understand that progressively adding techniques can broaden their skills and provide deeper insights.

User is especially interested in spaCy’s language models, word embeddings, feature extraction, and machine-learning classifiers. They have discussed sentence embeddings, averaged word embeddings, weighted representations, POS tags, dependency parsing, clustering, dimensionality reduction, and combining embeddings with other features. They want practical code and comparisons, including spaCy vs. NLTK and spaCy embeddings vs. Word2Vec/GloVe, as well as examples of SVM and logistic-regression sentiment classifiers.

Important technical caveats: spaCy’s standard pretrained pipelines such as `en_core_web_sm` do not directly provide sentiment predictions; sentiment requires a text-classification model (for example, `textcat`/Transformers) or another library. Common spaCy `*.md` vectors are static word vectors, while Transformer pipelines provide contextual representations. Avoid unsupported performance claims; results vary by versions, hardware, task, and model.
